newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Crichton thriller takes on air industry.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Crichton thriller takes on air industry.

text.p: This has been a tough few months for people who fear flying.

TWA Flight 800 exploded off the coast of Long Island on July 17, killing all 230 people aboard, prompting a still-inconclusive investigation into whether mechnical failure or sabotage brought the plane down. Two months before, on May 11, a ValuJet DC-9 plunged into the swamps of the Florida Everglades, killing all 110 on board.
Now one of America's most prolific and popular authors Michael Crichton has zeroed in on airline safety, a subject he says he started before the recent crashes.

His just-released novel "Airframe" centres around an investigation into why a fictional Norton Aircraft company plane bucks and dives through the air at 30,000 feet (10,000 metres), killing some people on board.
Crichton based his novel on a series of real-life incidents, including the 1979 case of a TWA 727 diving five miles (8 kms) straight down over Michigan before pilots recovered.

At issue in Crichton's book is an unexplained wing slat deployment on Trans-Pacific Airlines Flight 545, a fictional charter with a non-fiction problem. Layered on top of the mysterious deployment is manufacturer Norton's quest to keep the investigation secret, since the mishap was in international airspace, U.S. investigators are shut out.

A race to find the cause, without glaring television cameras, is the point of the book, not to scare readers. At least that's what the author says, despite his own jacket blurb hyping the "is it safe to fly" tagline.

Crichton has become a media presence of his own, gaining mega-star writer status on the tails of his fiction-turned-films "Jurassic Park," "Disclosure," "Rising Sun" and his "ER" television series creation.
He says the spotlight on air travel started after, not before he sat down to write "Airframe." Indeed, he says the glare of ValuJet could have scuttled his then-nascent project.

"I was well into by it by the time of the ValuJet crash. I panicked when I heard that because by then I was really liking the book. For the longest period I've been looking to talk about how the media affects the perception of reality," Crichton said.
"If ValuJet was an issue of slats deployment (which it wasn't) I would have had to either change the book enormously or abandon it."
Crichton plied away, accomplishing his goal of combining airplane manufacturing and the media. The book will be made into a film by Disney in the near future.
Crichton said he was able to see firsthand how planes are built at Boeing plants in the Pacific Northwest. A process the weak-kneed flyer may appreciate.

"My own experience in doing research was basically reassuring. I was very impressed with how carefully they're made, very impressed with how carefully even minor incidents are looked at," Crichton said.

What is not settled, in real life or the book, is the role government should play in a deregulated airline industry. Since 1978 American skies have been deregulated, and to some extent the skies are the limit for the number of no-frills airlines that pop-up and subsequently go under.
In the book Crichton gives a sharp slap at the shell airlines and the cosy industry-government relationship.

"Obviously deregulation is the favoured procedure, Europe is about to deregulate their industry, but it seems to me that we are in a sense coasting. The power is cut and we're gliding, for the moment everything is alright but we're not replacing the fleet as we used to," Crichton said.

"There are cost pressures on every aspect of the industry and I think we're going to have some sort of oversight because it's human nature, you can't expect people to have tremendous pressure on them and not to respond to the pressures."
